articles.title: Robotic Gait Multi-channel Mu Beta Neurofeedback Training in Paraplegics Enhanced Inter-regional Connectivity and Sensorimotor Functions.
articles.authors: Da Silva Serafini ER, Blanco-Diaz CF, Guerrero-Mendez CD, Bastos-Filho T, Dantas AF, Santo CC, Delisle-Rodriguez D.
articles.venue: IEEE transactions on neural systems and rehabilitation engineering : a publication of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society
articles.abstract: Complete spinal cord injury (SCI) that severely affects somatosensory and motor functions, greatly challenges advanced neuro-technologies and therapies addressed to repair neural system pathways and recover lost functions. Non-invasive solutions have been explored, reaching encouraging results. This study aims to explore the viability of a novel Neurofeedback (NFB) paradigm for enhancing the modulation of sensorimotor rhythms and cortical connectivity in a robotic-assisted gait training with complete traumatic and chronic SCI individuals. A motor imagery of gait therapy was conducted with Lokomat in two-stages of 12 electroencephalogram NFB sessions to teach the self-modulation of μ (8-12 Hz) and β (15-20 Hz) rhythms. First, a single-channel NFB over Cz using power bands was applied, and later a multi-channel NFB. This last consists of a brain-computer interface that accurately classifies when the individual is performing motor imagery of gait, and further computes μ and β power oscillations on the scalp surface covering motor and somatosensory areas. We observed in complete SCI individuals, improvements modulating power changes and inter-region connectivity for μ and β oscillations, as well as clinical gains covering motor functions, neurogenic bladder management, and functional independence. The encouraging outcomes open doors for developing brain-computer interfaces that empower and regulate both motor rhythms oscillations in brain areas which play an important role during lower-limb movements and walking.

articles.title: Sensory cortical disinhibition underlies long-term fear memory in humans
articles.authors: Joshua A. Brown, Yijia Ma, Yifan Wang
articles.abstract: Abstract How transient threats turn into persistent, long-term fear memories is a fundamental problem in neuroscience, yet the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. Early sensory cortex, traditionally viewed as a passive feature analyzer, is increasingly recognized as an active participant in fear processing. Combining high-definition α-frequency transcranial alternating current stimulation (HD α-tACS) with simultaneous EEG-fMRI (electroencephalography-functional magnetic resonance imaging) and transformer-based neural decoding, we tracked fear memory development across formation, consolidation, and long-term retention (assessed at 15 min, 24 h, and 7 days after fear conditioning). Spatiotemporal memory traces were identified at all three assessments, beginning at an early sensory stage (40–60 ms post-stimulus) and distributed across visual cortex and limbic regions. Conditioning potentiated occipital α-oscillation desynchronization, a marker of visual cortical disinhibition, which subsequently predicted the strength of long-term memory traces. Critically, targeted α-tACS over early visual cortex induced early visual cortical (V1/V2) inhibition, abolished conditioning-potentiated α desynchronization, and selectively disrupted fear-memory consolidation and retention while leaving initial acquisition intact. These findings establish sensory cortical disinhibition as a necessary mechanism for long-term fear memory in humans and identify early sensory cortex as crucial node for intervention of persistent maladaptive fear.

articles.title: Theoretical frameworks for credit assignment via behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity
articles.authors: Ian Cone, Claudia Clopath, Rui Ponte Costa
articles.abstract: Abstract Behavioral Timescale Synaptic Plasticity (BTSP) is a form of plasticity which drives place field formation in hippocampal pyramidal neurons. Unlike traditional learning rules, BTSP learns pre-post correlations on timescales of seconds and rapidly changes single-unit activity in only a few trials. To study how BTSP-like learning can be integrated into network models, we propose a generalized theoretical framework, gBTSP, which we apply to unsupervised and supervised tasks in feedforward and recurrent networks. We show that unsupervised gBTSP learns place field maps in the feedforward case and attractor memories in the recurrent case. For supervised learning, we derive how plateau events can reduce task error, enabling gBTSP to solve trajectory matching and delayed non-match-to-sample tasks. Finally, we find that the speed of credit assignment via gBTSP is limited by network depth or CA3-like recurrence, suggesting that additional mechanisms are necessary to account for BTSP-driven few-shot learning in naturalistic settings.

articles.title: The representational geometry of cognitive maps under cognitive control
articles.authors: Seongmin A. Park, Maryam Zolfaghar, Jacob Russin
articles.abstract: Abstract Recent work has shown that the brain abstracts non-spatial relationships between entities or task states into representations called cognitive maps. Here, we investigate how cognitive control enables flexible top-down selection of goal-relevant information from multidimensional cognitive maps retrieved from memory. We examine the relationship between cognitive control and representational geometry by conducting parallel analyses of functional magnetic resonance imaging data and recurrent neural network models trained to perform the same task. We find both stable map-like representations in a medial temporal lobe and orbitofrontal cortical network that reflect both task-relevant and irrelevant dimensions and context-dependent, orthogonal representations of only task-relevant dimensions in a frontoparietal network. These representational motifs also emerge with distinct temporal profiles over the course of training in the recurrent neural network, with map-like representations appearing first. We further show that increasing control demands due to incongruence (conflicting responses) between current task-relevant and irrelevant dimensions impact the geometry of subjective representations, and the degree of this effect further accounts for individual differences in cognitive control. Taken together, our findings show how complementary representational geometries balance stability and behavioral flexibility, and reveal an intricate relationship between cognitive control and cognitive map geometry.

articles.title: An Integrated Metacognition, Phenomenon-Based, and Inquiry Model for Critical Problem-solving and Self-Awareness
articles.authors: Chanaporn Rattanamalee, Phichittra Thongpanit, Nirat Jantharajit
articles.abstract: This research-and-development study developed and evaluated the content and structural suitability of an instructional model integrating metacognition, phenomenon-based learning, and inquiry for undergraduate students' critical problem-solving competency and self-awareness. In Phase 1, interviews with two instructors and nine students and observations of three general biology course sections at one Thai university identified a need for more explicit justification of alternative solutions and monitoring of thinking. These findings informed a six-component model with a five-step learning process. In Phase 2, five experts appraised the model and its assessment instruments. All 10 critical problem-solving items received an item-objective congruence (IOC) index of 1.00; the 18 self-awareness items received IOC indices of 0.60-1.00 (mean = 0.91). IOC-derived estimates of scale-level positive agreement (S-CVI/Ave proxies) were 1.000 and 0.956, respectively, under the reported distribution of expert judgments. The overall mean suitability rating for the model was 4.62 out of 5.00. The model positions evidence-based decision-making and metacognitive reflection particularly within Steps 4 and 5. The findings support the model's content and structural suitability in the studied context; learning-outcome effectiveness requires evaluation in implementation research.

articles.title: Body in memory: the role of bodily self-consciousness in episodic memory and autonoetic consciousness
articles.authors: Qiaoyue Ren, Andreea M. Gui-Bordeianu, Olaf Blanke
articles.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences
articles.abstract: Episodic memory (EM) enables the conscious recollection of personally experienced events, including contextual features such as visual, auditory and emotional details. However, the role of bodily signals has been largely neglected in EM, although the observer's body provides a rich bodily context during the encoding, storage and recall of events, and has recently been associated with a bodily form of self-consciousness (bodily self-consciousness; BSC). Here, we introduce key concepts and findings on BSC and then summarize recent experimental paradigms, as well as behavioural and neural evidence, on how BSC impacts EM. This includes autonoetic consciousness, a core EM feature that emphasizes the conscious re-experiencing of past events. Current evidence suggests that modulations of BSC impact later memory, including objective EM performance and subjective autonoetic recollection (and other forms of memory such as working memory). These BSC-EM effects are supported by brain mechanisms in the posterior parietal cortex (particularly the temporoparietal junction and precuneus), motor cortex (premotor cortex and supplementary motor area) and prefrontal cortex that are coupled with the hippocampal complex, mediating BSC effects in EM. Linking subjective bodily experience during encoding and retrieval to the subjective re-experiencing of past events, we highlight open questions for future research on self and memory. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self'.

articles.title: Uncertainty-Aware Embodied Artificial Intelligence with Hybrid Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Control for Resilient Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Systems
articles.authors: Babak Rahmani, Fatemeh Afghah
articles.abstract: Abstract Embodied artificial intelligence (Embodied AI) has rapidly emerged as a fundamental paradigm for developing autonomous robotic systems capable of perceiving, reasoning, and acting within complex physical environments. Recent advances in foundation models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures have significantly improved high-level semantic reasoning for robotics; however, their deployment in real-world field environments remains limited by distributional shifts, multimodal uncertainty, dynamic environmental changes, and the absence of safety-aware decision-making mechanisms. These challenges become substantially more pronounced in heterogeneous multi-robot systems operating under partial observability and communication constraints. This paper presents an uncertainty-aware embodied AI framework that integrates multimodal perception, shared latent world modelling, predictive uncertainty estimation, online self-supervised representation adaptation, and hierarchical decision-making through hybrid Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Control (RL-MPC). Unlike conventional embodied AI architectures that execute fixed perception and control pipelines, the proposed framework continuously maintains and updates an internal world representation, enabling adaptive reasoning, uncertainty-aware planning, and safe real-time control. Furthermore, the architecture naturally extends to heterogeneous teams of aerial robots, autonomous ground vehicles, and mobile manipulators through distributed latent representations that support cooperative perception, coordinated task allocation, and resilient autonomous behavior. The proposed framework is evaluated in photorealistic NVIDIA Isaac Sim environments containing randomized terrain geometry, vegetation density, illumination changes, dynamic obstacles, sensor degradation, communication uncertainty, and severe out-of-distribution conditions representative of realistic field robotic deployments. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements over vision-based navigation, reinforcement learning, model predictive control, and hybrid RL-MPC baselines. The proposed method achieves approximately 21% higher navigation success, reduces collision frequency by more than 35%, exhibits significantly improved robustness under increasing environmental uncertainty, and maintains stable cooperative performance across heterogeneous multi-robot teams. These results demonstrate that uncertainty-aware embodied world models, continual representation learning, hierarchical VLA-guided decision making, and hybrid learning-control architectures provide a scalable foundation for resilient embodied intelligence and represent a promising direction toward next-generation autonomous robotic systems operating safely and reliably in complex real-world environments.

articles.title: Coordination without command: active inference and the route to embodied intelligence
articles.authors: Alexander D. Shaw
articles.abstract: Embodied intelligence depends on bodies whose contact with the environment, distribution of load and capacity for action are only partly known and are changed by movement. We argue that this creates a practical reason to organize inference through distributed, hierarchical and plural processes, using active inference to relate local belief updating, contextual constraints and action selection within a common framework. The proposal brings together established ideas from factorized inference, distributed control and embodied robotics, distinguishing their mathematical description from the location of computation and authority over action. The octopus provides biological motivation through its combination of peripheral sensorimotor processing and central influences on behavior, while an articulated hexapod illustrates selected architectural choices through six leg-local predictive controllers coupled by neighbor messages and a shared mechanical body. The simulation includes intact locomotion and movement following programmed limb withdrawal and graph reconfiguration, although these observations do not isolate the contribution of inference or establish remapping. Together, the biological example and computational illustration clarify how local inferential processes may remain coordinated across bodily interfaces and timescales without a controller prescribing the complete joint trajectory.

articles.title: Language-related task-fMRI patterns and restorative online brain–computer interfaces in post-stroke aphasia: a protocol for a systematic review with voxel-based meta-analysis and narrative synthesis
articles.authors: Bin Shu, Jianming Fu, Keren He
articles.abstract: Background Post-stroke aphasia (PSA) can restrict everyday communication, social participation and access to rehabilitation. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) during language tasks (task-fMRI) identifies group-level regional activation patterns across distributed language networks, whereas restorative online brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) adjust feedback or training progression contingent on real-time neural signals. Here, restorative denotes a prespecified rehabilitation purpose rather than demonstrated therapeutic benefit. We will examine both evidence streams within language production and comprehension. Methods This protocol describes a systematic review incorporating voxel-based meta-analysis and a focused narrative BCI synthesis. Searches will cover PubMed, Embase via Embase.com, Web of Science Core Collection and APA PsycINFO via Ovid, adding IEEE Xplore for the BCI component. The primary task-fMRI outcome is spatial convergence of positive blood-oxygen-level-dependent responses for task > baseline during production in adults with PSA; comprehension serves as a secondary model. Spatial pooling requires at least 10 independent inputs per domain, accepting compatible whole-brain maps, complete signed coordinate sets, or confirmed whole-brain reports of no suprathreshold peaks in either direction. Domains below this minimum will be described without spatial pooling or vote counting. Eligible BCI studies must have a prespecified restorative aim and evaluate adults with PSA over at least two training sessions featuring online neural control, reporting a longitudinal neural outcome, an independent pre–post language or functional-communication outcome measured without online BCI assistance, or both. BCI implementation and outcomes will still be synthesized narratively when regional classification is not possible. Conclusion The review addresses three predefined objectives: identifying consistent task-fMRI convergence in PSA, describing trained neural features and reported clinical associations in restorative BCIs, and relating reported cortical BCI targets to peaks from the corrected task-fMRI meta-analysis for the corresponding language domain. Trail registration: CRD420261457995.

articles.title: From Egocentric Human Video to Robot Manipulation in the Era of Embodied Intelligence
articles.authors: Yi Wang, Jingqiu Wu, Lei Yao
articles.abstract: Egocentric human video (EHV) records close-range hand-object interaction (HOI) and the temporal structure of everyday activities, offering a potentially scalable source of experience for robot manipulation. Using this experience for robot control requires recovering useful supervision without recorded robot actions and accounting for differences in morphology, viewpoint, and action space. We define Ego2Robot learning as the process of learning or adapting robot manipulation policies from EHV, organized into four learning paradigms: explicit embodiment transfer, explicit action and task supervision, egocentric video representation pretraining, and latent action and dynamics modeling. The four paradigms differ in what they derive from human video: robot-format demonstrations, interpretable supervision, visual representations, or predictive models of actions and dynamics. For each paradigm, we trace what EHV information is extracted, how robot policies use it, and when the additional data is required. Besides, we review the benchmark datasets that cover EHV, robot demonstrations, and synthetic and simulated resources. This paper links EHV data's contribution to the task information preserved and the robot-specific grounding used during training or deployment. Finally, we identify challenges in physical feasibility, agent coordination, in-context adaptation, controlled evaluation, and predictive control.

articles.title: ActWorld-JEPA: Action-Conditioned JEPA World Models Meet Latent Planning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
articles.authors: Ziying Song, Shengkai Zhang, Caiyan Jia
articles.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) enable future prediction in latent space without pixel reconstruction. However, latent predictive consistency alone does not establish the relative driving quality of candidate plans. We present ActWorld-JEPA, a joint-embedding formulation for candidate-based driving. Where Plan-Conditioned JEPA (PC-JEPA) uses global and step-wise trajectory intentions to guide recurrent latent prediction, then combines the predicted future with the current scene through gated cross-attention; Relational Residual Reranking ($R^3$) models agreement and discrepancy between plan and future representations under planning supervision, yielding bounded, gated residual corrections to the base planning scores. This formulation connects latent prediction to candidate selection using only observed context and proposed trajectories at inference. Benchmark-specific implementations report 94.1 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, with the final selector calibrated using aggregate NAVTEST feedback, and 91.6 and 42.7 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and navhard, respectively. The nuScenes evaluation reports a mean $L_2$ error of 1.20 m and a predicted collision rate of 0.76% over 1--6 s. This work provides an effective path from JEPA's predictive representations to driving decisions informed by anticipated consequences.

articles.title: Building a robotic self
articles.authors: Martin V. Butz, Verena V. Hafner, Pablo Lanillos
articles.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences
articles.abstract: I wake up in the morning, I see my hand and I know it is me. This seemingly simple skill lies at the foundation of our agentive selves. We assume that the development of the self, in both biological and synthetic agents, is grounded in sensorimotor embodiment and inductive learning biases, as well as in the principle of predictive coding. Here, we explore the core inductive biases and process components for building a robotic minimal self. We propose that the formation of a hierarchical, generative model of the self is driven by active inference processes that interactively infer both an endogenous contextual frame and behaviour within this frame. Accordingly, experimental implementations in humanoid robots show how body ownership and agency can develop as foundational computational components. This work on building a robotic minimal self outlines future research directions in mechanistic modelling of the development of an artificial self. To probe the depth of this development, we sketch out embodied Turing tests that challenge complex problem-solving skills, as well as social intelligence and theory of mind. We suggest that uncertainty resolution and the social domain may be promising avenues for further research in the near future. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self'.

articles.title: Cognitive Cryptography Framework for Securing Brain Computer Interfaces Against Neural Signal Hijacking
articles.authors: Soufiane Ben Othman, Mustafa kakeeto
articles.venue: International Journal of Computational Intelligence Systems
articles.abstract: Brain–Computer Interfaces (BCIs) are rapidly transitioning from experimental prototypes to clinical and consumer deployments, exposing a novel attack surface: neural signal hijacking , wherein adversaries intercept, replay, or inject synthetic electroencephalographic (EEG) streams to compromise prosthetic actuation or infer private cognitive states. Conventional transport-layer security mechanisms fail to address the stochastic, non-stationary, and session-variant characteristics inherent to neural data. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Cognitive Cryptography Framework (CCF) , an end-to-end security architecture that co-designs neurophysiological signal processing with cryptographic primitives for context-aware authenticated encryption. At its core, CCF employs the Oscillation-Bound Frequency-Shift Keyed Hash (OB-FSKH) algorithm, which cryptographically binds epoch-specific session keys to a subject live neural oscillation fingerprint across five canonical frequency bands ( \(\delta\) , \(\theta\) , \(\alpha\) , \(\beta\) , \(\gamma\) ), ensuring automatic key expiration upon cognitive state transitions. Cryptographic entropy is harvested via a Cognitive Biometric Entropy Pool (CBEP) that distills high-fidelity min-entropy from inter-channel phase-locking values and band-power dynamics, seeding a forward-secret HKDF-SHA3-512 double-ratchet that formally guarantees IND-CCA2 confidentiality and EUF-CMA integrity under the random-oracle model. Concurrently, a lightweight Neural Anomaly Detector (NAD) leverages adaptive Mahalanobis distance scoring and Ljung–Box autocorrelation analysis to identify replay and generative injection attacks within a single 250 ms epoch. Extensive empirical validation across two benchmark datasets (BCI Competition IV Dataset 2a and PhysioNet Motor Movement/Imagery) under four adversarial scenarios demonstrates a mean authentication accuracy of 98.7 %, a replay-detection recall of 99.2 %, and an injection-detection \(F_1\) score of 0.987, while incurring only 4.3 ms of deterministic computational overhead per 64-channel epoch on a Raspberry Pi 4 edge node. By unifying neural-context binding, biometric key derivation, and real-time statistical anomaly detection, CCF establishes a clinically viable, low-latency security paradigm for next-generation neural prosthetics, closed-loop neurofeedback systems, and augmented-reality BCI deployments.

articles.title: A multi-session simultaneous EEG-fMRI dataset with repeated experience sampling
articles.authors: Lotus Shareef-Trudeau, David Braun, Tiara Bounyarith
articles.abstract: The integration of electroencephalography (EEG) and functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) can be used to characterize temporal and spatial components of neural activity during unfolding mental experience. Here we introduce a multi-session simultaneous EEG-fMRI dataset with measures of continuous behavior and spontaneous mental experience. Data components, organized in Brain Imaging Dataset Structure (BIDS) format, include fMRI, EEG with carbon wire loop sensors for artifact removal, continuous performance task responses, experience sampling ratings, and mental health surveys, from 24 healthy adults. Tasks included the gradual-onset continuous performance task and resting state with intermittent experience sampling of 13 unique thought dimensions (36 repetitions, including 468 total ratings, per participant). The same protocol was completed on two different days, yielding approximately 1.33 hours of simultaneous EEG-fMRI data per individual. The dataset may be used to explore the behavioral and experiential relevance of brain activity during the wakeful resting state. The dataset also provides a means to study the reliability of relationships between fMRI and EEG features across sessions within individuals.

articles.title: NVC-DSDNet: neurovascular coupling-aware delay alignment and subspace disentanglement network for hybrid EEG–fNIRS brain–computer interfaces
articles.authors: Shunyao Wang, Yunyuan Gao, Zhengnan Zhang
articles.abstract: Hybrid EEG–fNIRS brain–computer interfaces combine rapid electrophysiological activity with hemodynamic information, but neurovascular latency and entangled multimodal features hinder effective fusion. We propose the Neurovascular Coupling-Aware Delay Alignment and Subspace Disentanglement Network (NVC-DSDNet), which couples delay-aware attention with shared–private neural subspaces. EEG responses serve as temporal anchors that retrieve task-relevant fNIRS features over candidate delays, while Neural Feature Subspace Decomposition separates shared neural intent from modality-specific information. An adaptive multi-head decision module then weights unimodal and fused predictions at the sample level. In subject-independent five-fold cross-validation, NVC-DSDNet achieved accuracies of 72.67% for motor imagery, 82.79% for mental arithmetic, and 76.17% for word generation. Learned delay weights peaked at 4.5–5.5 s for motor imagery and shifted to 6.0–9.0 s for mental arithmetic, consistent with task-dependent hemodynamic time courses. These results show that coupling-aware temporal alignment and subspace disentanglement can improve multimodal neural decoding while retaining neurophysiological interpretability.

articles.title: Cholinergic blockade reveals a role for human hippocampal theta in memory encoding but not retrieval.
articles.authors: Gedankien T, Kriegel J, Zabeh E, McDonagh D, Lega BC, Jacobs J.
articles.abstract: Cholinergic dysfunction is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease and other memory disorders. Yet, the neurophysiological mechanisms linking cholinergic signaling to memory remain poorly understood. In this study, we administered scopolamine, a muscarinic cholinergic antagonist, to neurosurgical patients with intracranial electrodes as they performed an associative recognition memory task. When scopolamine was present at encoding, we observed disruptions to hippocampal slow theta oscillations (2-4 Hz), with selective impairments to recollection-based memory. However, when scopolamine was present during retrieval alone, we observed disruptions to slow theta without impaired memory performance. These disruptions included dose-dependent reductions in theta power, theta phase reset, and encoding-retrieval pattern reinstatement. Together, our results challenge the notion that theta oscillations are necessary for memory retrieval, and instead suggest that theta universally reflects an encoding-related neural state. These findings motivate updates to current models of acetylcholine's role in memory and may inform future therapies targeting rhythmic biomarkers of memory dysfunction.

articles.title: Knowledge Sharing and Lifelong Learning in Multi-Intelligent Agent Systems: A Distributed Knowledge Update Framework Based on Graph Neural Network
articles.authors: Yunlan Xue, Weixing Wang, Gang Chen
articles.abstract: In this paper, an end-to-end distributed knowledge updating framework based on graph neural network is proposed to deal with the problem of knowledge islands and catastrophic forgetting in multi-agent systems. The framework includes adjacency subgraph digger, which is used to capture topological evolution and inject structural semantics; meta-learning scheduler, which adaptively adjusts gradient step size and synchronization rhythm to optimize communication; cross-task memory distillation module, which integrates incremental regularization and self-supervised replay to stabilize historical knowledge; and a containerized fault-tolerant mechanism to support rapid recovery after node deactivation. Experiments on OGB, OpenLORIS-Continual and Ego-Motion data sets, DGL-CUDA cluster, and ROS-TurtleBot2 cluster show that this method can quickly converge and effectively alleviate the performance degradation under communication constraints and topology changes, which provides a universal, reusable, and potential solution for multi-agent lifelong learning.

articles.title: PAIR: Proprioception-Aligned Image-Ray Representations for Viewpoint-Robust Manipulation
articles.authors: Sung-Wook Lee, Xuhui Kang, Dylan Losey
articles.abstract: While imitation learning has made substantial progress toward generalizable robot manipulation through scaling, viewpoint robustness remains a major bottleneck. Visuomotor policies rely heavily on visual inputs, yet images provide an inherently ambiguous signal under viewpoint change: similar scenes may appear markedly different across viewpoints, while distinct states may share certain visual overlaps. A policy must therefore infer not only the task-relevant state, but also how it is visually projected under a particular camera configuration. This entanglement of viewpoint-dependent appearance and task-relevant state can make learning inefficient and limit generalization to unseen viewpoints. Recent work has begun to address this challenge through camera-ray conditioning and representation learning using geometric cues to induce invariance. However, providing camera information as additional context does not by itself ground visual representations in how the task scene is visually projected, while geometric alignment without camera context can introduce spurious correspondences by ignoring viewpoint-dependent projection. We propose PAIR, a contrastive learning framework that aligns joint image-ray representations using robot proprioception. PAIR encourages observations with similar robot states to remain close in representation space across viewpoints, providing a structured grounding signal for learning viewpoint-robust features. PAIR is a highly adaptable framework: it can be used to train Diffusion Policy (DP) or post-train vision-language-action (VLA) models. In simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks with camera variation, PAIR consistently outperforms the behavior cloning baseline without ray conditioning by 12.7% and 26.7% points, respectively, demonstrating stronger generalization to unseen viewpoints. Project website: PAIRrobot.github.io.

articles.title: Backpropagation-Free Continual Learning: A Unified Energy-Based Framework, Reproducible Benchmark, and Open Challenges
articles.authors: César Hernando Valencia Niño
articles.abstract: Backpropagation has been the dominant credit-assignment mechanism behind the deep-learning revolution, yet it is global, memory-hungry, biologically implausible, and costly on hardware dominated by data movement. In parallel, predictive coding, equilibrium propagation, contrastive Hebbian learning and forward-only schemes have shown that useful credit assignment can also arise from local variables and the relaxation of an energy function. This manuscript is a review with a reproducible benchmark, not a proposal of a new learning rule. We organise existing backpropagation-free methods and continual-learning strategies under a common Local Equilibrium Learning (LEL) formulation, re-validate the core theoretical links numerically, and use a controlled continual-learning benchmark as an auditable case study within the review. The theoretical contribution is unification and verification, not priority over predictive coding, equilibrium propagation or replay. The empirical contribution is diagnostic rather than exhaustive: a benchmark of catastrophic forgetting with local networks that makes the review reproducible. We compare regularisation (EWC, SI), noise replay and generative “dreaming” across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 in two independent implementations. Generative replay with local generators turns class-incremental Split-MNIST forgetting (chance level, the same as EWC and SI) into 86.8±0.2%, which is 96% of the joint-training ceiling and 97.4% in the task-incremental setting; the same mechanism reaches 82.0% on Fashion-MNIST and 37.0% on CIFAR-10. A matched control that holds the retention mechanism fixed and swaps only the learning rule shows that backpropagation with the same generative replay reaches a comparable or slightly higher accuracy than LEL (90.3% vs. 86.7% class-incremental); the benefit is attributable to generative replay as a retention mechanism, not to the local learning rule itself, which we state plainly rather than let the headline number imply otherwise. The CIFAR-10 number is intentionally reported as a limitation of a shallow raw-pixel local model, not as a claim of competitiveness with modern CNNs or transformers trained by backpropagation. We separate positive results; negative results and open limitations; and release scripts, seeds, dataset preparation and configuration files so that this paper can serve as an honest entry point for backpropagation-free continual learning.

articles.title: FOE-Dreamer: Deployment-Efficient Learning of Cyber Defense Policies in Operational Networks
articles.authors: Yinuo Du, Christopher D. Kiekintveld
articles.abstract: Autonomous cyber defense is widely studied with deep reinforcement learning, but most work trains policies inside simulators because learning requires many trial-and-error interactions. Simulator-based training carries a fidelity gap: trained policies face authentication delays, partial action failures, service dependencies, and user traffic patterns that the simulator did not represent, and degrade on transfer. Training directly in the network being defended removes the gap but makes every interaction slow and costly, so sample efficiency becomes the binding constraint. Model-based reinforcement learning has reduced sample requirements on games and physical robots by orders of magnitude by planning inside a learned world model, but it has not been applied to defenders trained in operational networks. We present FOE-Dreamer (Factored Opponent-Enhanced Dreamer), a model-based reinforcement learning framework that trains a defender online and directly in a network on cloud infrastructure, without a simulator stage. FOE-Dreamer separates three sources of variation in the latent state: a controllable component driven by defender actions, an exogenous component driven by benign user activity, and an opponent embedding inferred from defender-observable signals alone. Separating the components reduces the variance in policy gradients during planning in imagination. Against two scripted attacker profiles with user activity emulated by the GHOSTS framework on an 8-host OpenStack testbed, FOE-Dreamer trains within a 3-day budget on a single GPU and achieves about 2$\times$ better episode loss than Rainbow and IQN baselines under matched compute. Both the factoring and the opponent model contribute to the gain, and the learned latents are consistent with the intended separation.

articles.title: Could metacognitive therapy be a contender for first-line treatment for functional neurological disorder? The case for clinical trials
articles.authors: Nikki S. Scheiner
articles.abstract: Metacognitive Therapy (MCT), grounded in a model first proposed more than three decades ago (Wells & Matthews, 1994), has been used to treat a range of mental health disorders and, more recently, extended to physical health conditions, including Long Covid (Johnson et al., 2024). This Opinion article argues for controlled trials to evaluate whether MCT should now be offered as a first-line treatment for functional neurological disorder (FND). Current Hallett et al, 2011Hallett et al, , 2016;;LaFrance et al, 2014.) In patients prone to somatosensory amplification, repeatedly focusing on illness beliefs may heighten threat-driven attention to bodily sensations, reinforcing the very hypervigilance that maintains their symptoms (Barsky & Silbersweig, 2023;Kube et al, 2020).Metacognitive therapy, by contrast, focuses on increasing the patient's awareness of their thinking styles and relationship with their thoughts. By discouraging extending thinking about thought content, MCT arrests the self-reinforcing feedback loops that maintain psychological distress and pathological coping. Regaining flexible attentional control frees individuals to reengage with their external world, rebuild agency, and modify detrimental higher order regulatory processes. Similarly, the FND literature proposes that excessive attention to the body disrupts normally automatic movement, and that reducing this hypervigilance may allow automatic motor function to resume (Edwards et al, 2012).Functional symptoms are common: anxiety, for example, may bring a dry throat, sweating palms, abnormal breathing, increased heart rate, and gastric disturbance. When their frequency, intensity and/or duration (over 6 months) interfere with daily functioning, treatment is indicated. Until DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013; text revision 2022), these impairments were typically termed Medically Unexplained Symptoms, Hysteria or Conversion Disorders. The first term reflected a diagnosis of exclusion. The second and third signalled the legacy of Charcot and Janet at the Salpêtrière Hospital in nineteenth-century Paris and of Freud's emphasis on repressed conflict.Today, FND sits within the DSM-5 chapter on Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders, alongside other functional conditions in the cognitive, sensory, and motor domains. Individuals may experience symptoms across multiple organ systems, supporting the 'lumper' case for a polysyndromic phenotype. Functional presentations may overlay organic conditions (as with |Functional Seizures and Epilepsy) or co-exist with unrelated medical conditions. Symptoms may be positive (gastric disturbance, tremors, pain) or negative (weakness, fatigue, numbness). For the purposes of this piece, Functional Neurological Disorder (FND) denotes all functional disorders.The failure of the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) to produce dedicated guidelines for the treatment of FND in England and Wales creates an opportunity to consider MCT as a candidate intervention. UK treatment delays (currently eight years) reflect the lack of a clear classification system, limited resources, and a historical knowledge deficit among clinicians, who often conveyed their view that symptoms were imagined or feigned. Patient factors include the condition's stigma and repeated requests for multiple medical tests and investigations, resulting in iatrogenic harm.Functional patients, 70% of whom are women, account for about a third of new outpatient presentations and up to half of GP appointments. The most recent figures for England put the annual NHS cost of treating functional conditions at £2.89 billion (then about 10% of its budget). A further £14 billion was attributable to illness benefits, sickness absence, reduced productivity, and impaired quality of life (QoL) (Bermingham et al., 2010). Bass and Pearce (2016) reported distress and disability in this group, comparable with that severe and enduring mental illnesses.In DSM-5 (2013), the criteria for somatic symptom disorder were recast to foreground positive clinical features: internal inconsistency/variability and symptoms incompatible with (neuro)anatomical pathology. The previous requirement of a psychological trigger (trauma or abuse) gave way to a focus on the patient's active-inference/illness beliefs and consequent behaviours , such as bodily hypervigilance illness-reinforcing coping. Clinicians have observed the same mechanisms (Phillips, 2025). This reorientation aligns closely with metacognitive theory, in which distress is maintained by the Cognitive Attentional Syndrome (CAS). The CAS consists of perseverative worry or rumination, threat monitoring (such as inward-focused attention) and unhelpful coping strategies, driven by maladaptive metacognitions. The CAS is MCT's primary target.MCT's efficacy already has a strong evidence base. What perhaps makes it particularly suitable for the treatment of functional and other somatic related disorders is that it shares the biological Bayesian model's understanding of how distress is induced and maintained. In the Bayesian framework, priors (expectations drawn from past experience) anticipate sensory input, with any discrepancy yielding a prediction error. This error updates the prior into a 'posterior,' which then becomes the new prior. The computational process continues until a Bayes-optimal decision is reached. Edwards et al. (2012) argued that a prior shaped by previous experience of illness, distorts the weighting of lower-level data, overriding the prediction error. The inference may be Bayes-optimal inference but, because the priors are aberrant (idiosyncratically biased), the outcome (a functional impairment) does not fit realworld data. As these processes happen outside conscious control, functional symptoms are experienced as involuntary. Although largely untested, the Bayesian model is increasingly used to explain the onset and maintenance of functional conditions.Metacognitive therapy maps comfortably on to the Bayesian model: both frameworks describe a multi-level architecture in which higher-order structures generate top-down expectations shaping lower-level processing. Their levels of explanation differ: MCT addresses psychological and experiential processes, while Bayesian inferences describe a cascading hierarchy of neural and computational ones. Even so, both converge on distress as the outcome of stochastic overweighting (high confidence that the prediction is correct) and fixated attention. Wells's (2009) metacognitive model, grounded in the Self-Regulatory Executive Function (S-REF) model (Wells & Matthews, 1994), posits that metacognitions (beliefs about one's own thinking) direct higher-order processing, governing the selection and appraisal of incoming data. Bottom-up sensory data from the body or the environment (for example, a percept or the absence of normal feeling) are briefly registered in working memory. There they give rise to thoughts processed in object mode, that is, taken as direct reflections of reality (for example, 'This sensation is not normal: I am unwell'). Prolonged inward-focused attention keeps these lower-level thoughts, images or perceptions of illness in constant iteration. This strengthens them and consolidates maladaptive metacognitions (for example, the belief that worry about symptoms is necessary for safety). The mind's natural tendency towards emotional homeostasis is thereby overruled. In turn, an internal view of the Self and the World that resists disconfirmation, frequently related to illness vulnerability, triggers a positive (self-reinforcing) feedback loop. Input incompatible with this mental model is appraised as 'noise' (not signal) and, like Bayesian prediction errors in functional disorders, suppressed. Wells's (2009) model traces a cyclic process in which the CAS is fuelled by both higher-and lower-order processes. The model identifies a Comparator, which assesses the discrepancy between the individual's current (distressed) state and their desired state (for example, achieving a sense of safety or certainty). The Cybernetic Code then selects a 'remedy', mobilizing the individual's familiar, self-defeating coping strategies, a key component of the CAS. Once these strategies are activated, the feedback loop intensifies and, paradoxically, strengthens the certainty of danger, leaving the individual with the belief that their worries are uncontrollable.Unlike the Bayesian model, MCTprovides both an explanation and a therapeutic framework.Staying in metacognitive mode fosters patient engagement and helps identify the metacognitions that drive distress.Although I argue for its suitability for DSM-5-TR's (2022) Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders, MCT does not require a psychiatric diagnosis. Freedom from a nosological framework distance it from the DSM-5-TR's continued labelling Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder as 'Conversion Disorder', albeit in brackets. Freud's legacy, the view that physical symptoms stem from unconscious conflict, may encourage patients with functional symptoms to self-stigmatise. MCT's diagnosis-free approach sidesteps that stigma.MCT restores choice and agency to patients overwhelmed by beliefs that their worries or rumination are uncontrollable. Anxiety, a contributory maintenance factor for some patients in FND, becomes less threatening as the individual learns that contrary to their previously beliefs, they can flexibly control their attention.Wells has developed two core techniques to target the CAS and undermine dysfunctional procedural/implicit knowledge. Detached Mindfulness trains patients to view their thoughts as products of consciousness (mental phenomena) separate from their sense of self.Individuals learn that their constant stream of thoughts is like water running freely in a sink; left alone, it drains away. It is only when they attribute importance to them (putting the plug in) do the thoughts build up and eventually overflow. This simple realisation often suffices to undermine the salience (in Bayesian terms, precision weighting) previously attributed to their beliefs and metacognitions.The second technique targets excessive attention, the engine of the feedback loop. The Attention Training Technique (ATT) disrupts the positive metacognition that certainty can only be achieved through chronic bodily hypervigilance (self-focused attention) together with constant worry, avoidance, and/or reassurance seeking. ATT normalises human experience, reminding the individual that negative thoughts or worries may intrude but need not derail them: they can simply notice them before returning to their goal. With increased cognitive capacity for goals and tasks, efficiency, productivity, and mood improve, whilst the fatigue accompanying many functional disorders may lessen.What next? The search for a unitary explanation for FND continues. Physicians' lack of diagnostic certainty and the historical neglect of research into female predominant disorders are cited as significant factors in the under-funding of this common condition (McLoughlin et al, 2023). Notwithstanding the fragmentation of care, there is growing evidence that individuals with functional movement disorders can be successfully treated with specialist physiotherapy, bypassing talking therapies altogether. LaFrance's CBT protocol for managing functional seizures is a validated treatment that returns agency to patients. (LaFrance et al, 2014). Other patients with functional disorders may opt for exploratory, cognitive-behavioural or values-based approaches, while still others will decline all therapeutic offers. Unknown numbers never reach tertiary services, attending only the Emergency Department or their own doctor. Many, usually men, are believed to be misdiagnosed with less stigmatizing conditions. (McLoughlin et al, 2023).Patients frequently come to therapy feeling stigmatized. Many report being repeatedly dismissed by consultants unfamiliar with functional symptoms (Kannan, 2009). For these groups, psychoeducation provides an important opportunity for them to air their grievances as well as restore their belief that treatment may be effective. Metacognitive Therapy does not typically offer psychoeducation about the aetiology of conditions and avoids being drawn into debates about the patient's view of their own condition. Instead, it actively discourages patients from ruminating about their experiences, viewing rumination as part of the CAS. This may be seen as a limitation. However, sharing the formulation-linking the presenting complaint to the patient's CAS processes that maintain it (in MCT terms, bridging) -may strengthen the therapeutic alliance and improve outcome. Moreover, the gold-standard practice of embedding therapy within a multidisciplinary framework allows psychoeducation to be provided elsewhere in the patient's care.Research into the biological underpinnings of FND (specific biomarkers, neurobiological mechanisms) and the evaluation of candidate therapies proceed along parallel, independent tracks. In the UK, however, CBT has become the default psychotherapy, reflecting its historical primacy. I argue that this has resulted in institutional inertia and -despite variable outcomes -a monopoly that disadvantages patients [CITATION?]. In a recent article, Marano and Mazza (2026) state that a core element of successful CBT protocols is 'addressing the metacognitive awareness of symptom awareness ' (p. 15). Yet, although some protocols incorporate decentring techniques, CBT's core targets -Negative Automatic Thoughts (NATs), Rules for Living and Core Beliefs -remain object-mode thoughts.The burden of FND on the sufferer, the Exchequer and society is huge and largely avoidable.MCT is acceptable to a majority of patients. It is parsimonious, transdiagnostic and evidencebased, showing large effect sizes and stable gains across mental health disorders (Andersson et al., 2025). Recent trials have highlighted its success in treating physical health conditions, including Long Covid, a condition that shares maintenance factors with FND. Furthermore, its understanding of distress reflects current research on the triggers and maintenance factors of FND. These considerations now warrant controlled trials of MCT in FND, so that it can take its place alongside other psychotherapies in relieving the physical and emotional suffering of this common yet undertreated disorder.

articles.title: Electrolytic-microbubble dynamics delineate safety thresholds during intracortical microstimulation with flexible neural interfaces
articles.authors: Iliasov Artem, H F Ma, F H Li
articles.abstract: Abstract Intracortical microstimulation (ICMS) with ultraflexible neural electrodes enables low-threshold, chronically stable, and high-resolution modulation of neural circuits, providing a promising strategy for sensory restoration and closed-loop neuromodulation. However, the microscopic mechanisms delineating its safe and effective current range remain unclear. Here, we combine intravital two-photon (2P) imaging and electrophysiology in awake mice to examine the current-dependent neurovascular outcomes of charge-balanced stimulation via ultraflexible arrays. We observed gas bubbles formed along the electrode during ICMS, with bubble size increasing quadratically with current amplitude, consistent with a Faradaic bubble-growth model. Intravital 2P imaging reveals that at low-to-moderate currents (20–40 µA), vascular leakage is small, spatially confined, and largely reversible, whereas higher currents (≥60 µA) induce a sharp transition to extensive, field-dominated extravasation and secondary vessel disruption. This transition coincides with immediate, stimulus-locked motor responses and the onset of electrode degradation. Multiphysics simulations reproduce the observed nonlinear leakage–current relationship by incorporating gas bubble–induced electric field redistribution and voltage-dependent vessel wall permeability. The model indicates that gas bubbles act as local electric-field modulators, concentrating suprathreshold fields near the bubble boundary at lower currents while shielding more distant vessel segments; at higher currents, this confinement breaks down and the system enters a field-dominated damage regime. Collectively, these findings define a mechanistically informed safety window for ICMS with flexible neural interfaces and identify bubble-assisted vascular permeabilization as a key failure mode at high currents, crucial for the design of future bidirectional brain-computer interfaces and high-precision neuroprosthetic protocols.

articles.title: Reduced entorhinal and dentate theta-gamma coupling associated with adult Reelin loss in Alzheimer’s disease relevant mice
articles.authors: Neehar Girimaji, Murat S. Durakoglugil, Joachim Herz
articles.abstract: Early Alzheimer’s disease (AD) affects entorhinal-hippocampal circuits, motivating functional measures of altered network coordination. We examined local field potentials and multiunit activity in head-fixed mice in a virtual-reality (VR) environment, comparing WT, App NL-F , and App NL-F -Reln-cKO groups ( n = 3 male mice per genotype). Reelin deletion was induced in adulthood using a ubiquitous tamoxifen-inducible Cre driver and was not restricted to entorhinal cortex (EC). Recordings sampled EC, dentate gyrus (DG), and CA1. Theta–gamma phase–amplitude coupling was quantified using modulation index (MI) and phase-locking value (PLV) between theta phase and the phase of the gamma-amplitude envelope. Nominal genotype effects were detected for DG-theta/DG-gamma coupling (MI, p = 0.034; PLV, p = 0.035) and EC-theta/DG-gamma coupling (MI, p = 0.0043; PLV, p = 0.0079), with descriptively lower means in App NL-F -Reln-cKO mice. Regional power spectra appeared broadly similar; a nominal genotype effect was reported for DG theta power ( p = 0.029), rather than a selective DG gamma-power reduction. Exploratory analyses suggested stronger coupling attenuation in the 35–55-Hz range and lower DG-associated coupling in both high and low theta/delta states. These findings identify DG-associated theta–gamma coupling as a candidate functional readout of adult Reelin loss in an AD-relevant background. The small cohort, uncorrected comparisons, widespread deletion, and absence of coupling–behavior analyses limit anatomical and functional inference.

articles.title: Research on Solid Motor Performance Prediction Method Based on Deep Meta Learning
articles.authors: Huixin Yang, Fanbin Meng, Cheng Chen
articles.abstract: Total impulse characterizes the overall propulsive capability of a solid rocket motor. The cost and resources required for ground static firing tests limit data availability, while temperature-dependent thrust variations complicate modeling with few records. This study develops an MT model that combines model-agnostic meta-learning with a Transformer. Complete thrust records are divided into three segments using the thrust peak and an amplitude threshold, then downsampled. The model receives the compressed sequences and their actual timestamps, extracts temporal relationships through self-attention, and learns a shared initialization from high- and low-temperature tasks. This initialization supports total impulse prediction from a small set of ambient-temperature records. Model comparisons, sampling analyses, and cross-temperature validation assess the use of compressed thrust information and historical operating-condition data. With three-segment, 500-point inputs, MT achieves a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 0.429511% on the ambient-temperature query set. Record-level error analysis and cross-temperature validation show that information learned from high- and low-temperature tasks improves ambient-temperature total impulse estimation with limited target records. Combining sequence representation with task adaptation improves the use of existing temperature-specific test data for few-shot total impulse prediction and motor performance analysis from compressed records.

articles.title: STRIDE: Continual Learning using Skill Transfer and Reuse with Incremental Discrete Encoding
articles.authors: Pranav Agarwal, Michele Rocca, Victor Brian Zordan
articles.abstract: Developing general-purpose physics-based character controllers via reinforcement learning is fundamentally hindered by policy interference in continuous spaces. While training isolated controllers avoids interference, it incurs significant training overhead and yields disjointed behavioral transitions. To address these challenges, we present STRIDE (Skill Transfer and Reuse with Incremental Discrete Encoding), a framework for the continual learning and composition of diverse character behaviors. Instead of training independent models, STRIDE leverages policy quantization via a Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) to dynamically discover and encode reusable behavioral primitives within a discrete latent space. New behaviors and tasks are learned by combining existing codewords, providing a stable motion prior that structurally eliminates catastrophic forgetting. Evaluated across diverse locomotion styles, agile maneuvers like kicking, and composite tasks like target-aiming, STRIDE accelerates downstream learning by × 1.3 to × 2.0 compared to baseline learning frameworks. Furthermore, the discrete representations inherently improve policy interpretability, allowing direct tracking of skill activations and behavioral decisions during task execution. STRIDE offers a scalable, transparent solution for continual character control without compromising motion quality.
